# The Thread (blind-pass generation, 2026-08-06)

I am, I'm afraid, one of those people who cannot follow a plot.

I lose the thread. I say that without thinking about it, and so do you, and neither of us has ever wondered
what thread we mean or who was holding the other end of it. But there is a thread, and it is a very old one,
and it is still lying about in the middle of the English language where anybody might trip over it.

The word is *clue*.

A clue used to be a *clew*, and a clew was a ball of yarn. That is all it was. If you had wound your wool
into a sphere, you had made a clew, and there was nothing mysterious about it at all — no detective, no
magnifying glass, no body in the library.

Then Theseus went into the labyrinth.

You will remember the arrangement. There is a maze, there is a Minotaur in the middle of it, and there is
the awkward fact that killing the Minotaur is only half the problem, because the other half is getting back
out again. Ariadne, who is cleverer than everybody else in the story, hands Theseus a ball of wool. He ties
one end to the door. He unwinds it as he goes. He kills his monster, he picks up the thread, and he follows
it home.

He followed the clew. And because that story was told and retold for two thousand years, the word for the
wool became the word for the thing that gets you out of a maze, and then the word for any small hint that
gets you out of any confusion at all, and now a clue is what a detective finds under a hedge and has not
been made of wool since roughly the reign of Elizabeth.

I find this cheering, and not only because I like knowing things at parties. I find it cheering because the
metaphor was never really retired. It was only forgotten. We still *lose the thread*. We still *follow* a
line of argument. A story still *unravels*. A plot — and here the language is being almost insultingly
obvious — is something you *unwind*.

Which brings me to the useful part, and I promise there is one.

When a reader tells you they got lost in something you wrote, you will be tempted to believe they are
telling you it was too complicated. That is almost never what happened. Difficult things are read happily
every day by people who have no business understanding them. What happened is that you let go of the wool.

Somewhere around the third paragraph you stopped tying each sentence to the one before it, and the reader,
who had been holding on quite loyally up to that point, found that there was nothing in their hand. They did
not put the piece down because it was hard. They put it down because it had stopped being connected.

So the fix is not to simplify. Simplifying a piece that has lost its thread produces something that is both
thin and still confusing, which is the worst of all available outcomes. The fix is to go back to the last
place where the reader was definitely still with you — and it is always earlier than you think — and to run
the wool forward again from there, sentence to sentence, without letting go.

Ariadne's real gift was not the wool. Anybody can produce wool. Her gift was understanding that the man
walking into the maze would be a different man on the way out: brave enough going in, and completely lost
coming back, and in no condition to reason about left turns.

Your reader is that man. Give them something to hold.
